Analysis: As Trump dismisses AI concerns, Albanese tries to show he's in control
The details were thin, but the vibe was clear.
Before departing this week for a round of international summits, the prime minister announced a new set of "mandatory AI safety and security protections".
In truth, these were more a set of worthy principles to somehow hold someone somewhere to account when something goes wrong — like an AI agent going rogue and hacking into a government website.
But exactly who (or what) would be held responsible, and how they would be punished, remains a work in progress.
Acting Prime Minister Richard Marles tried valiantly yesterday to explain how this might work. In theory.

"I think this will be a case of looking at the prompts that are involved in the circumstance, the way in which the AI agent is constructed … and ultimately bringing that back to the decisions, the human decisions, that have been taken by the owners of this technology or the developers of this technology," he told the ABC's Hamish Macdonald.

Plibersek 'confident' first home buyers will be able to afford a house
Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek says she's "confident" that over time, first home buyers will be able to afford a house to live in.
The federal government's May budget unveiled changes to negative gearing and the capital gains tax discount.
Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) data on home loan applications shows a sharp decline in the number of new investor loans.
Lending applications for owner-occupiers are 9.8 per cent lower than a year ago, and lending to first home buyers is 12.3 per cent lower than 12 months ago, according to the data.
Plibersek has told News24 while there are fewer home loan applications, first home buyers make up a larger share of them.

"They're a bigger share of a smaller number, which shows that the market's rebalancing back towards home ownership," Plibersek says."I am confident that what we will see over time is people being able to afford a house to live in, which is what the housing market should prioritise."

"I am confident that what we will see over time is people being able to afford a house to live in, which is what the housing market should prioritise."
Turnbull defends COP31 brew-haha
Australia can't pour fresh cups of coffee fast enough at its taxpayer-funded cart on site at COP31 in Turkiye.
Such is the popularity of the Aussie flat white that delegates attending the UN climate conference have proven more than willing to line up for an hour just to get a free brew.
The Coalition has been highly critical of the federal government's $32,000 outlay on the coffee cart, despite the idea dating back to Opposition Leader Angus Taylor's time as energy minister.
But at COP31 overnight, a new unexpected defender of the cart emerged in the form of Malcolm Turnbull.
Though the former prime minister's first response was to admit, "I don't actually drink a lot of coffee", he remains a fan of the freebies at the conference.

"I think this is one of the smartest things the Australian government does at COPs because everyone knows Australian coffee is the best, and it gets people to the pavilion," he said."All the dollars that are spent on marketing here, that is probably the best dollar spent because it gets people to come to the Aussie pavilion."
"I think this is one of the smartest things the Australian government does at COPs because everyone knows Australian coffee is the best, and it gets people to the pavilion," he said.
"All the dollars that are spent on marketing here, that is probably the best dollar spent because it gets people to come to the Aussie pavilion."
Finnish ambassador says he never thought planning day would lead to viral meme
The Finnish ambassador to Australia says he and his team had no idea an embassy planning day would lead to a viral social media meme.

The Finnish Embassy in Canberra posted a reel on Instagram this week, accompanied by a song from Finnish composer Jean Sibelius, saying the diplomatic mission would be temporarily closed on November 10.
The meme went viral on social media, with other Finnish diplomatic missions and even the Finnish foreign minister playing into it.
As my colleague Clare Armstrong reported, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Finnish President Alexander Stubb joined in on the joke from COP31.
Finnish ambassador to Australia Arto Haapea has told ABC News Breakfast members of his team started receiving messages during their planning day.

"We started the planning day quite normally. We went through what a successful year that we've had this year all the visits and then how do we build on that for next year," Haapea says."And then people started getting messages, like hang on there's something happening on Instagram and elsewhere, so that was very positive."
"We started the planning day quite normally. We went through what a successful year that we've had this year all the visits and then how do we build on that for next year," Haapea says.
"And then people started getting messages, like hang on there's something happening on Instagram and elsewhere, so that was very positive."
So are there any other Finnish embassy closures planned? Haapea says not for now.
It seems the embassy has become a bit of a tourist attraction here in Canberra. Haapea admits the embassy received a few visitors yesterday checking to see if the embassy was open.
Finnish PM reassures Albanese about Canberra embassy
Who'd have thought a meme sparked by the Finnish embassy in Canberra would make it all the way to the highest levels of government so fast?
Barely a day after Finland went viral after innocently announcing a routine one-day closure of its Australian embassy, the leaders of both countries have joined in on the joke.
President of the Republic of Finland Alexander Stubb has shared a selfie with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on the sidelines of COP31 in Türkiye overnight.
"I have confirmed to the Prime Minister of Australia Anthony Albanese that the Finnish Embassy in Canberra is open," Stubb posted on Instagram.
Pocock welcomes new AI safety and security standards
David Pocock has welcomed the federal government's moves to introduce safety and security standards for artificial intelligence.
This week, Labor announced it would introduce the mandatory standards and a new regulator with the power to impose penalties on tech companies that fail to comply.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, the independent ACT senator says he would like to see stronger mandatory reporting requirements.

"Finally, they're saying we do need safeguards, which seemed obvious to everyone who was paying attention. Now it is a case of ensuring that we actually strengthen what the government is proposing," Pocock says.

"I'd like to see far stronger recommendations around the need for mandatory reporting. And the report uses words like 'consider or explore such actions'. This is clearly urgent and needs to happen now."
David Pocock says Labor budget changes are working
Independent senator David Pocock says he thinks Labor's budget measures aimed at getting investors out of the housing market are working.
In May's federal budget, the federal government made changes to capital gains and negative gearing tax settings to help more first home buyers get into the market.
The latest lending data shows lending to owner-occupiers is 9.8 per cent lower than a year ago, and lending to first home buyers is 12.3 per cent lower than 12 months ago.
The data also shows a sharp decline in the number of new investor loans.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Pocock says he thinks the government should now work on delivering affordable social housing.
"For too long, housing has just been seen as this investment vehicle, this asset class, rather than as something that is fundamental to human flourishing," Pocock says.

"And so if you look at the drops, a lot of the bigger drops are coming from the top end of the market, which saw eye-watering increases over the last five years."I do think there is a role for the government to now really step up with a renewed focus on the supply of public, social, and genuinely affordable housing. But I think big picture, this is a change that had to happen."

Key Event
Employment minister says lending data is promising for home supply
Employment Minister Amanda Rishworth says the latest lending data shows investors are purchasing new homes compared to 12 months ago.
Australian Bureau of Statistics released data showing lending to owner-occupiers is 9.8 per cent lower than a year ago, and lending to first home buyers is 12.3 per cent lower than 12 months ago.
Asked on ABC Radio National Breakfast whether the government's budget measures have contributed to the decline, Rishworth says the shift in the data on investor purchases is promising.
"When it comes to this data that we've got in front of us, what we've seen, if you drill down into it, is a concentration of that reduction being in investors buying existing houses," Rishworth says.

"There's been a shift to investors investing in new housing, and that's a good thing because that does add to supply."We want to see more home owners, first home buyers, into their own home, and our policies are certainly geared towards that."

"We want to see more home owners, first home buyers, into their own home, and our policies are certainly geared towards that."
Rishworth won't say if government will aim for net savings in mid-year budget update
Employment Minister Amanda Rishworth has refused to say whether the government believes achieving net savings would help reduce inflation.
Australia's inflation rate jumped to 4.3 per cent over the year to September, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics.
The federal government has been under pressure to reduce inflation and has refused to commit to net savings in the mid-year budget update.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Rishworth has indicated the government won't be moving to cut services for Australians.

"Both the treasurer and the prime minister have indicated we will take a responsible approach to budgeting, of course, at the same time, making sure that Australians get the services that they need. This is a responsibility of government," Rishworth says.
Key Event
Rishworth talks up latest ABS lending data
Workplace Relations Minister Amanda Rishworth has talked up the latest lending data released yesterday.

Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) data released yesterday shows lending to owner-occupiers is 9.8 per cent lower than a year ago, and lending to first home buyers is 12.3 per cent lower than 12 months ago.
Labor changed the tax rules in May's federal budget that mean investors can only access negative gearing (from budget night) if they purchase a new home and contribute to housing supply.
Speaking to ABC News Breakfast, Rishworth says the figures showed investors were pivoting to purchasing new homes.

"Probably the biggest concentration of reduction was in investors buying existing homes and that means a shift towards investors buying new homes. That, of course, is important, it adds to supply," Rishworth says."But also a shift towards home ownership and we want to see more home ownership. That's been a focus of our government through our policies and that's a good thing."

"Probably the biggest concentration of reduction was in investors buying existing homes and that means a shift towards investors buying new homes. That, of course, is important, it adds to supply," Rishworth says.
"But also a shift towards home ownership and we want to see more home ownership. That's been a focus of our government through our policies and that's a good thing."
AI best practice guide highlights how workers can benefit from technology: Rishworth
The federal government has released a draft best-practice guide for the adoption of artificial intelligence in the workplace.
Labor says it will aim to provide businesses with a practical roadmap on how to manage AI investment into their workforce.
Workplace Relations Minister Amanda Rishworth says the guide highlights the shared benefits of adopting AI in the workplace.

"The first point of call is work out what the problem is. Speak with workers about where their pain point is in their job. Is it tasks? Is it the tedious tasks that distract them from actually doing the part of the job they really enjoy?" Rishworth says.
"What this guide is about is how do you make sure that workers can see the benefit of it [AI]? ... People have got to see how it does help them with their job, not actually make it more difficult."
She says the data currently available shows AI is not having an economy-wide impact on white-collar jobs.
Rishworth says David Jones should look to redeploy workers amid store closures
The workplace relations minister has urged department store David Jones to work closely with its employees as it moves to close stores.
Yesterday, the retailer confirmed it would be closing 19 of its 38 stores across the country and New Zealand before the end of the year.
The department store was placed into administration last week after negotiations with major landlord Westfield broke down.
Amanda Rishworth has told ABC News Breakfast she hopes the company can restructure and redeploy its workforce.

"It's obviously a very difficult time for those workers and certainly I would urge David Jones to work with its workforce to look at how many of those workers can get redeployed in other stores," Rishworth says.
McKenzie takes aim at Labor over latest lending data
Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie has urged the government to reverse its May budget tax changes following the release of lending data.
Speaking to Channel Nine, McKenzie says the government needs to revisit its changes to capital gains tax and negative gearing.

"For a country like ours, we're built on home ownership. It's the greatest asset that Australians have. We've really seen the Labor Party betray that great Australian dream of home ownership through their budget," McKenzie says.
Key Event
Gallipoli, Gaza and AI on agenda as Albanese meets Erdoğan

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has met Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan on the sidelines of COP31 in Antalya, with the leaders discussing the conflict in the Middle East, artificial intelligence and defence cooperation.
The pair talked about their joint leadership of this year's climate summit and efforts to turn international climate commitments into practical action.
According to a readout of the meeting, they also discussed the economic impact of the conflict in the Middle East and the need for de-escalation, as well as security cooperation in the Indo-Pacific.
Growing trade and investment ties, aviation links and efforts to protect children online were also raised.
Key Event
Albanese discusses clean energy, AI and online safety with Norwegian PM
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has met with his Norwegian counterpart Jonas Gahr Støre on the sidelines of COP31 in Türkiye.

Clean energy investment was a key focus, with Albanese encouraging Norwegian companies and the country's sovereign wealth fund to invest in Australian renewable energy, storage and green iron projects.
The leaders also discussed online safety, including Australia's Digital Duty of Care legislation and Norway's proposed social media age restrictions.
AI safety was also on the agenda, with both leaders emphasising the importance of keeping advanced AI models under human control and oversight.
According to a readout of the meeting, the pair also discussed support for Ukraine, the conflict in the Middle East and Indo-Pacific security.
Australia faces climate leadership questions at COP31 as PM calls for Pacific aid
Australia's bid to lead global climate action has drawn criticism over its continued fossil fuel expansion, as Anthony Albanese calls on world leaders to help protect the Pacific.

The prime minister used the opening of the COP31 Leaders Summit in Antalya, Türkiye, overnight on Wednesday to urge countries to step up climate action and support vulnerable nations, warning Pacific communities were "pleading" for assistance.

But his appeal came as United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres delivered a forceful warning that the world must stop building new fossil fuel infrastructure, while climate advocates accused Australia of undermining its international leadership by continuing to expand coal and gas production.

Australia is sharing a leading role in this year's climate negotiations with host nation Türkiye, with both countries seeking to secure practical agreements on electrification, climate finance and adaption.
